questions.q: I will be at the station at ten.
questions.why: The future of 'be' is regular: אֶהְיֶה, תִּהְיֶה, יִהְיֶה, נִהְיֶה, and the prefix א־ already says 'I', so אֲנִי is optional. An hour takes בְּ: בְּעֶשֶׂר.
The prefix נ־ marks 'we' in the future, and the root's א falls silent behind it: נֹאכַל, like אֹכַל for 'I will eat'. The question word comes first, as in English.

a: נוֹעָה אַף פַּעַם לֹא שׁוֹלַחַת תְּמוּנוֹת.
נועה [אף פעם לא|לעולם לא] שולחת תמונות
נועה לא שולחת תמונות אף פעם
questions.why: Never is אַף פַּעַם, and like every Hebrew negative word it keeps its לֹא before the verb. The root ends in ח, which turns the feminine ending into two pataḥs: שׁוֹלַחַת, not שׁוֹלֶחֶת.

questions.q: Noa doesn't know who is writing to her.
a: נוֹעָה לֹא יוֹדַעַת מִי כּוֹתֵב לָהּ.
questions.why: A question word can open a clause inside a sentence with no change of order: לֹא יוֹדַעַת מִי כּוֹתֵב. 'To her' is the לְ with an ending: לָהּ.

questions.q: Will you come to Tel Aviv tomorrow?
questions.why: The future 'you' is ת־ in front: תָּבוֹא to a man, תָּבוֹאִי to a woman, תָּבוֹאוּ to several. The prefix says who, so the pronoun can go.

questions.q: Do you know how to send a picture?
questions.why: Knowing how is יוֹדֵעַ with an infinitive straight after it, and no word for 'how' is needed: יוֹדֵעַ לִשְׁלוֹחַ. In the present the pronoun stays, because the verb does not say who.

questions.q: He will call her, like always.
questions.why: Hitpa'el keeps its תְ after the future prefix: יִתְקַשֵּׁר. The person you call takes לְ, so 'her' is לָהּ.

questions.q: I won't say anything about the picture.
a: אֲנִי לֹא אַגִּיד כְּלוּם עַל הַתְּמוּנָה.
questions.why: The verb לְהַגִּיד is hif'il with its root's נ hidden in the dagesh: אַגִּיד, תַּגִּיד. After לֹא, the word כְּלוּם means 'anything'.

questions.q: Nobody will be at home tomorrow.
a: מָחָר אַף אֶחָד לֹא יִהְיֶה בַּבַּיִת.
מחר אף אחד לא יהיה בבית
אף אחד לא יהיה [מחר בבית|בבית מחר]
questions.why: Nobody is אַף אֶחָד, and Hebrew keeps a לֹא beside the verb as well. It counts as one masculine person, so the verb is יִהְיֶה.

questions.q: Tomorrow there will be a lot of people at the station.
questions.why: The present יֵשׁ never changes, but its future agrees with what there will be: אֲנָשִׁים is plural, so יִהְיוּ.

questions.q: We won't have a car tomorrow.
questions.why: Future having is יִהְיֶה לְ, but the verb agrees with the thing had: מְכוֹנִית is feminine, so תִּהְיֶה. The לֹא goes in front of it.

questions.q: Tomorrow Grandpa will write to Noa, and she will answer him.
a: מָחָר סַבָּא יִכְתּוֹב לְנוֹעָה, וְהִיא תַּעֲנֶה לוֹ.
[מחר סבא|סבא מחר] יכתוב לנועה [ו|]היא תענה לו
סבא יכתוב לנועה מחר [ו|]היא תענה לו
questions.why: Pa'al future has an o in its stem: יִכְתּוֹב. The root of עָנָה ends in ה, so its future ends in ־ֶה, תַּעֲנֶה, and it takes the person answered with לְ: לוֹ.

questions.q: Tomorrow I will see Grandpa at the station, and we will eat together.
a: מָחָר אֲנִי אֶרְאֶה אֶת סַבָּא בַּתַּחֲנָה, וְנֹאכַל יַחַד.
questions.why: Grandpa is a known person, so like any name he takes אֶת. The prefixes carry the person, א־ for 'I' and נ־ for 'we', so both pronouns are optional.

questions.q: When she sees the message, she will smile.
a: כְּשֶׁהִיא תִּרְאֶה אֶת הַהוֹדָעָה, הִיא תְּחַיֵּיךְ.
questions.why: After כְּשֶׁ Hebrew uses the future where English uses the present: כְּשֶׁהִיא תִּרְאֶה is 'when she sees'. Both halves of the sentence are future.

questions.q: When I have time, I will call you.
a: כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִי זְמַן, אֲנִי אֶתְקַשֵּׁר לְךָ.
questions.why: Having in the future is יִהְיֶה לִי, and after כְּשֶׁ it stays future where English says 'when I have'. The שֶׁ doubles the letter after it: כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה.
